rv.q: Gough is flinty and fierce and utterly compelling as she descends into derangement.
It is Gough, though, that holds this evening. Every move she makes is precise, vital, mesmerising.
This histrionic, hyper-stylised version from director Ebenezer Bamgboye may be aiming to recapture some of that original confrontational force, but overshoots the mark.
This revival lives and breathes through the temperature of its performances, with Gough's Abbie and Momoh's Eben ensuring the farm's suffocating heat feels palpable.
But while you can’t help admire his heated, guttural vision, it stretches out the play’s action and ultimately threatens to overwhelm the drama it seeks to illuminate.
In the end, both play and production strain for a level of feeling and meaning it can’t quite capture.
Desire Under the Elms is well acted with stunning lighting and focused direction. Yet there was something missing.
Indeed the 2 hour and 40 minutes running time (including interval) vastly outstays its welcome.
Bamgboye’s production features a bewildering mix of bronze lighting, intrusive music, shouting and random dance sequences which obscure any meaning or message behind the classic.
It has an interesting story at its heart with the potential to shock and move, but it's bogged down with excess dialogue and can't punch through.
I could appreciate the intensity of what was unfolding without always feeling emotionally connected to it.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this overwrought but visually striking O'Neill revival. Atmospheric lighting and live music impress, but Bamgboye's hyper-stylised direction divides critics, with many finding it excessive and the pacing sluggish.
